attributes.label: Hotter, drier summers
attributes.description: Meteorological drought (KNMI'23): higher evaporation, summer precipitation deficit, and lower river discharge.

attributes.label: Sea-level rise
attributes.description: Rising sea level (KNMI'23 scenarios); increases hydrostatic pressure of marine water on polders and estuaries.

attributes.label: Wetter winters
attributes.description: Increased winter precipitation, providing potential recharge volume if retained.

attributes.label: Rainwater lens  recharge in the low  polders
attributes.description: The rain that soaks in and refills the rainwater lenses of the low polders: mostly the winter's rain surplus, since in summer most of the rain evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). On Schouwen-Duiveland upward saline seepage keeps it within the clay top layer of the low polders, and tile drains carry much of it off during each rain; recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island).
attributes.sources:
van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953a). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: I. Salt. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(3), 153–163. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17866
de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.label: Rainwater lens  thickness in the low  polders
attributes.description: The thickness of the fresh rainwater lenses on top of the saline groundwater in the island's low polders, from the surface to the middle of the mixing zone between them: about 2 m on average in the low-lying polders with saline seepage, under 2 m over more than half of the 56 km² surveyed (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island from a helicopter and on the ground). These lenses keep salt out of the root zone and reach only the crop on their own field. A Stock: a year's recharge barely moves it (Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders).
attributes.sources: de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.label: Land subsidence
attributes.description: Peat oxidation and clay consolidation caused by low drainage levels, lowering the land surface relative to sea level.

attributes.label: Polder surface  elevation (NAP)
attributes.description: Physical land surface elevation of the polder (-1.5m to -3.5m NAP), lowered by subsidence. Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014, p. 15); near Zierikzee the water holds under 10 mg/l, mostly fine sand, and its salt marshes rise 3–10 mm a year (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004, pp. 14, 27), against 16–32 mm on young marshes along the Westerschelde (De Mesel et al., 2013).
attributes.sources:
De Mesel, I., Ysebaert, T., & Kamermans, P. (2013). Klimaatbestendige dijken: Het concept wisselpolders (Rapport C072/13). IMARES Wageningen UR. https://www.vliz.be/imisdocs/publications/289823.pdf
Ma, Z., Ysebaert, T., van der Wal, D., de Jong, D. J., Li, X., & Herman, P. M. J. (2014). Long-term salt marsh vertical accretion in a tidal bay with reduced sediment supply. Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science, 146, 14–23. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecss.2014.05.001

attributes.label: Root zone salinity
attributes.description: The salt concentration of the soil water in the crop root zone. Salt harms a crop in two phases: at once osmotically, slowing the growth of young leaves, and more slowly as sodium (Na+) or chloride (Cl-) builds up in the leaves, ageing the older ones early (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656, a review of plant physiology, which holds wherever the crop grows). It rises in a dry summer as the soil dries out and salt rises by capillary rise, and falls with the winter's rain surplus, which washes the topsoil of well-drained soil free of salt in one winter and that of badly drained soil in two or three (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155–158, measured after the floods in Zeeland): within the year where the soil drains well, so an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources:
Munns, R., & Tester, M. (2008). Mechanisms of salinity tolerance. Annual Review of Plant Biology, 59, 651–681. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.arplant.59.032607.092911
van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953a). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: I. Salt. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(3), 153–163. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17866

attributes.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
attributes.description: The upward flow of salt groundwater from the sand below into the clay and peat top layer of the island's polders, in mm a day, which leaves through drains, ditches and evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3662). The higher water pressure at depth drives it in the low polders, where it keeps the rainwater lenses thin, mostly under 2 m, and the shallow groundwater brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10); below the lens its water holds 10 to 16 g of chloride a litre (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675), against about 16 to 17 g in North Sea water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Most of Duiveland gets salt seepage, most in its low parts near the Oosterschelde (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 27); in the western low polders it is strongest near the Grevelingen and the Oosterschelde (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The flow follows the water pressures, which change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Soil structure
attributes.description: The soil's aggregates and pores, which set how fast water soaks in: well-drained clay with its structure intact let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely, while clay whose structure sodium had broken down became impervious and sticky when wet (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, measured after the floods in Zeeland). A Stock: once broken down, it recovers over years (Root zone salinity → Soil structure). Workability, which structure and wetness both shape, is Spring workability of the fields.

attributes.label: Upconing of salt  groundwater
attributes.description: Upward cone of the salt-freshwater interface beneath pumping irrigation wells as the freshwater lens thins.

attributes.label: Farmers' demand for  deep polder drainage
attributes.description: Farmers' wish for low ditch levels, so that their fields drain: dry enough in spring for heavy machinery to work them, which holding water back for dry times makes hard (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44), and free of water damage after heavy rain, which farmers in the island's western low polders often find a bigger problem than drought (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). They put it to the water board as it prepares its water level plans, which it does with interest groups such as farming, and in views on a draft (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17): on Duiveland's draft of 2021, four views feared that a raise the plan proposed to study would bring more flooding in extreme rain (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53). Within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Fresh water supplied  to the island
attributes.description: Fresh water brought to the island's farms from outside it in the growing season (present in Tholen and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, the Bevelanden and Schouwen-Duiveland). It needs a supply route, and in drought it is what the national distribution leaves for the route to carry. Rijkswaterstaat makes that distribution: in drought it divides the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes among the users through weirs, pumping stations and sluices, by the verdringingsreeks when there is too little for all, and the greater part of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply (Rijkswaterstaat, n.d.).
attributes.sources: Rijkswaterstaat. (n.d.). Verdeling water bij droogte. Retrieved November 6, 2026, from https://www.rijkswaterstaat.nl/water/waterbeheer/droogte-en-watertekort/verdeling-water-bij-droogte

attributes.label: Freshwater  availability for crops
attributes.description: Fresh water crops can draw on in the growing season: rain, the soil moisture and groundwater of the field above the lens, water farmers pump or have stored, and water supplied from outside, which reaches the island nowhere now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources: Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.label: Freshwater storage  measures
attributes.description: The fresh water a year that the measures in place on the island's farms keep, store or collect for the growing season. They work three ways (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 16–23, 53, for the island): in the low polders, controlled drainage, anti-salinisation drainage (Drains2Buffer) and weirs in ditches keep the thin rainwater lens against salt, the water staying in the field's own soil, where it cannot be pumped (pp. 33, 53); on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay, the creek-ridge infiltration system, the Freshmaker and underground storage under a clay layer infiltrate winter water to pump in summer (pp. 20–22, 38); and double drainage collects fresh drain water into a basin to irrigate from (pp. 23, 29, 32). An adaptive practice: measures to keep more fresh water in the ground as drought and salinisation increase (p. 4). The study found them not yet fitted to the island and too risky for many farms to invest in alone (pp. 4, 11). A Stock: a measure, once built, lasts 15 to 30 years (pp. 17–22, 34). The farm decides a measure; infiltrating water needs the water board's permit or a notification, a weir the neighbours' consent, and raising a ditch's level the water board's cooperation (pp. 26, 44–45). Whether a farm wants to store weighs storing against its other ways through a dry summer (pumping, other crops), where capacity to invest is whether it can. Stored water pays back over years, which suits a farm that owns its land more than one on a short lease; and where stored water spreads under the neighbours, one farm pays and others gain. Whether either holds a farm back is a question for the group model building session.
attributes.simplification: Counts the measures of three kinds as one quantity, the fresh water a year they keep, store or collect, each kind reaching crops by its own link out: to Winter rain drained away, to Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes, and to Freshwater availability for crops. It assumes every kind responds alike to the drivers into this element. Every loop through it keeps its polarity and its mechanism; what it leaves out is that a rise in one kind need not be a rise in another, so the semi-quantitative analysis cannot vary them apart.
attributes.sources: Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.label: Groundwater extraction  for irrigation
attributes.description: Fresh water farmers pump from the fresh groundwater through their own wells, to irrigate in summer; the water board's pumping stations belong to drainage. How much and from where is Pumping the water board allows. Whose lens a well draws on, the farm's own or one it shares with its neighbours, so that a farm pumping less leaves water to them, is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the rules are written so that a well's effects stay within the farm's own field (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021), an aim of the rules rather than a measurement. Pumping follows the season's shortfall within the year: an Auxiliary.
attributes.actors: Arable farmers on Schouwen-Duiveland, Waterschap Scheldestromen
attributes.sources: Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland. (2021, June 9). Antwoorden op vragen van de statenleden Heerschop en Van der Vliet (PvdA) inzake onttrekkingen grondwater (zaaknummer 54188, aanhangsel tot de notulen van Provinciale Staten nr. 191). https://www.zeeland.nl/sites/default/files/digitaalarchief/IB21_ae4d5ac6.pdf

attributes.label: Objections to land-use  plans
attributes.description: Objections, appeals at the Council of State (Raad van State) and political pressure against plans for the island's water and land, the water board's water level plans among them, which slow, change or stop a plan.

attributes.label: Winter rain drained  away
attributes.description: Rain in winter that field drains carry off instead of refilling the rainwater lens: in the low polders tile drains carry much of it off during each rain (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island). It follows each rain, within the year: an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources: de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.label: Crop yield
attributes.description: Physical yield per hectare of conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) under the prevailing freshwater, soil and workability conditions; what salt takes from their harvest is Harvest lost to salt. The island's arable farms grow potatoes, onions, sugar beet, cereals, grass seed and vegetables in rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30, 38, from the farms studied), and some in the low polders have stopped growing sown onions for the salt (p. 31). A season's harvest: an Auxiliary.
attributes.simplification: The current crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) are one yield per hectare. Each yields less with a larger water shortfall, worse soil structure or fields that cannot be worked in time, so every link into the yield keeps its sign for each crop and no loop through it changes. What one yield leaves out: the crops lose in different proportions (the yield response factors on Crop water shortfall → Crop yield), and farms can shift their rotation among them, as some in the low polders stopped growing sown onions for the salt.
attributes.sources: Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.label: Market demand for  alternative crops
attributes.description: Consumer demand and offtake contracts for novel salt-tolerant or alternative crops (e.g. protein crops).

attributes.label: Local processing  capacity for new crops
attributes.description: Plants and supply chains on or near the island that store, process or sell new salt-tolerant crops. Breeding of tolerant varieties is Salt-tolerant varieties on offer. Buyers and processors build or keep it where they find it worthwhile against processing the crops elsewhere.
attributes.actor: Buyers and processors of the island's crops
attributes.actors: Buyers and processors of the island's crops

attributes.label: Adoption of new  salt-tolerant crops
attributes.description: Hectares under crops new to the island's rotations that tolerate salt (quinoa, samphire, sea aster), which need other machines, knowledge and buyers than the current crops. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them.

attributes.label: Agricultural land  value
attributes.description: The price farmland sells for (€/ha), set by what buyers expect it to earn; banks value it as collateral in their own risk assessment.
attributes.simplification: A soil's structure enters the land's value only through what the land earns (Soil structure → Crop yield → Farm income → this element), the sign the same, since buyers price what they expect it to earn. What it leaves out: any value a buyer gives good soil beyond its income.

attributes.label: Risk premium on farm  loans
attributes.description: The interest banks charge arable farms above their own funding cost, for the risk they see in the loan.
attributes.actor: Banks lending to the island's farmers
attributes.actors: Banks lending to the island's farmers

attributes.label: Basel IV capital  requirements
attributes.description: European banking regulations requiring stricter risk weighting on loans when climate/soil risks reduce collateral value. The EU sets them: its banking package (CRR III/CRD VI) puts the final elements of the Basel III standards of 2017 into EU law, the new rules of the Capital Requirements Regulation applying from 1 January 2025, those of the directive once each member state has transposed them (European Commission, Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union, 2023).
attributes.sources: European Commission, Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union. (2023, December 14). Latest updates on the banking package. https://finance.ec.europa.eu/news/latest-updates-banking-package-2023-12-14_en

attributes.label: Dependence on  high-margin  salt-sensitive crops
attributes.description: The share of high-value, salt-sensitive cash crops (seed potatoes, onions) in the rotation, which a farm with high debt payments needs to keep up its income, and which the machines and know-how it would lose by switching tie it to.

attributes.label: Farm income
attributes.description: Farms' revenue from crop sales, set by yield and prices, minus their costs (the water board's levy, interest, their own pumping), per hectare in a year.
attributes.actors: Arable farmers on Schouwen-Duiveland, Waterschap Scheldestromen

attributes.label: Farmers' capacity to  invest
attributes.description: What a farm has left to invest after its debt payments and rent, beside the credit a bank will give it.
attributes.actors: Arable farmers on Schouwen-Duiveland, Banks lending to the island's farmers

attributes.label: Financial leverage
attributes.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020).
attributes.actors: Banks lending to the island's farmers
attributes.sources: van der Meulen, H., van der Meer, R., & van Asseldonk, M. (2020). Financiering transitie naar duurzame landbouw: Inzicht in het huidige financieringslandschap en ontwikkelingen (Rapport 2020-097). Wageningen Economic Research. https://edepot.wur.nl/532092

attributes.label: Arable land in the  polders
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's land farmed as arable land, with conventional or salt-tolerant crops, whoever owns it. It falls when land that changes hands goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land; what the land becomes then (nature, grassland, water storage) waits for the group's system boundary.

attributes.label: Crop water shortfall
attributes.description: What crops need in the growing season beyond the water they get: the gap farmers' water decisions respond to. What a crop needs, whatever the water's origin, is the water it uses when it has enough, its evapotranspiration, set by the weather (radiation, air temperature, humidity and wind speed) and by the crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). The island's farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders; with no link to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought in and no ditches flushed in dry periods, so the farms run short of water, as the dry years 2018, 2019 and 2020 showed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.
attributes.sources:
Allen, R. G., Pereira, L. S., Raes, D., & Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration: Guidelines for computing crop water requirements (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56). FAO. https://www.fao.org/4/x0490e/x0490e00.htm

Deltares. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.label: Freshwater supply  route to the island
attributes.description: Pipes or channels that could bring fresh water to the island, as their capacity in a summer; none exists. Who decides on one and who pays is on the facts list under External freshwater supply; news reports say the province has costed a pipeline (unread at the source). IenW shapes it twice: its minister allots the Delta Fund, from which a freshwater region can claim 25% of a regional measure's cost, up to 50% for an innovative one or one carried out by several regions (Algemene Rekenkamer, 2026, p. 31); and the Delta Programme 2027, under the Delta Commissioner's direction and presented by the minister with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes that the south-west delta's areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, the region open to exploring small extensions of the supplied area that add evident value, are future-proof and keep the extra demand on the Volkerak-Zoommeer limited, the demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet not raised (Ministerie van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat et al., 2026, pp. 88–89).
attributes.sources:
Algemene Rekenkamer. (2026, September 3). Zorgen over zoetwater: Onderzoek naar de voortgang van het Deltaprogramma Zoetwater. https://www.tweedekamer.nl/downloads/document?id=2026D40892

attributes.label: Spring workability of  the fields
attributes.description: Whether heavy machinery can work the fields early in spring without damaging the soil, set by soil structure and by how wet the soil is: soil work done when the soil is too wet smears and compacts it and forms clods, and more rain in spring leaves fewer moments to do it (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, from the Dutch cultivation guides, on potatoes). It follows the soil's wetness within the season, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Polder drainage depth
attributes.description: How far below the surface the water board holds the ditch levels in the island's polders (the drooglegging), as its water level plans set them: Duiveland's plan sets a target level for each of its level areas, from 0.8 to 2.7 m below NAP, in most the summer level higher than the winter one, against nature's order, to prevent water damage in winter and drying in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 63–64). It moves from the winter level to the summer one in steps in March and April, as the weather and the farmers' soil work allow (p. 66). On a creek ridge studied for water storage the depth is over 1.5 m in winter in large parts (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 42). The depth holds until the board carries out a new plan: Duiveland's plan of 2021 replaced one from 1982 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 24), and the board checks each plan every three years and renews it at 17 years or once it no longer fits (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17), so a Stock. Where the land subsides under a level held, the depth shrinks until a new plan lowers the level, as the board has done where there is peat (2025, p. 13).

attributes.label: Water board's plans to  raise ditch levels
attributes.description: The water level plans in which Waterschap Scheldestromen raises a polder's ditch levels, from the draft until their levels take effect. The board matches its levels to the land's use and soil, its principle that the level follows the land use: arable land 80 to 120 cm below the surface by soil, permanent grassland 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29; 2025, pp. 5, 7), weighing flooding, drought, fresh water and groundwater (2021c, p. 19), subsidence (2025, pp. 13–14) and a change's costs against its benefits (2025, p. 12). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, where levels had been kept low to store extreme rain, to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (2021a, p. 69). The general board adopts each plan (2025, p. 18); of its 30 members, 26 represent the residents and two the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, appointed by ZLTO's board (Reglement voor het Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, arts. 6–7). A plan waits years for the works its levels need (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Polder drainage depth), so a Stock.

attributes.label: Harvest lost to salt
attributes.description: The conventional crops' harvest that salt in the root zone takes, over the island's fields still under them, in a season. On the island, farms where seepage pressure is high and the surface water is salty all year have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Zeeland is among the coastal provinces where potatoes and barley lose considerable yield to salt (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). Salt's effect on yield builds up over weeks to months and is read over the season (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Freshwater lens  thickness under creek  ridges and dunes
attributes.description: The thickness of the fresh groundwater under the island's sandy creek ridges and dunes, down to the middle of the mixing zone with the saline groundwater: 5 to 15 m under the creek ridges (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island), reaching about 30 m under the creek ridges and the dunes and nearly 100 m under the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). The lens farmers pump: wells are allowed only in fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick (p. 26), and it reaches crops through those wells alone (pp. 20–22, 26, 38, 53); on the higher fields above it salt is no problem, the saline seepage there being weak (p. 31). A Stock: it grows and thins over years (Freshwater storage measures → this lens).

attributes.label: Pumping the water  board allows
attributes.description: The volume the island's farms may pump a year under Waterschap Scheldestromen's rules. Where: from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). How: a horizontal well at most 6 m below the surface and 80 to 200 m long, at least 200 m from the next well and 50 m from a neighbour's field. How much: at most 800 m³ per hectare and 8,000 m³ per well a year, set at what rain recharges so the fresh-salt boundary does not rise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b). Extractions rose in recent dry years, and the province and the water board talk of registering the volumes more precisely (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021); no source read shows the farms' pumping changing the rules, the 2026 revision keeping the cap. A Stock: a notified well pumps until the board forbids it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b).

attributes.description: What the island's farmers, their advisers and contractors know of how freshwater storage works on the island: how the soil and groundwater behave, and what a measure costs, risks and yields. It builds up as measures are built and monitored, so a Stock.

attributes.description: Summer precipitation deficit and high evaporation reduce natural recharge.
Higher sea level increases hydrostatic pressure beneath dikes.
More winter precipitation increases potential infiltration into the soil.
Higher winter rainfall peaks are mostly discharged under conventional drainage.

Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673). So a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens.

attributes.description: Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3662, 3667, 3673, 3675, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). On Duiveland the salt water reaches into or almost into the root zone in places (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 26). Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: A thicker freshwater lens buffers against salt upconing under wells.

Holds in the low polders, where the thin rainwater lens keeps the topsoil fresh, which makes farming possible there (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10, for the island): water a measure keeps in the lens reaches only the crop on that field, as groundwater and soil moisture, and lies too deep for its roots at germination (p. 33), when most of the island's shortfall falls (pp. 27, 31); later in the summer the soil supplies a well-established crop (p. 27). The lens under the creek ridges and the dunes reaches crops only through wells (pp. 26, 38), which is Groundwater extraction for irrigation → Freshwater availability for crops. Within the season.

A rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders is not yet sourced.

attributes.description: Higher polder elevation reduces the hydraulic head difference driving upward saline seepage.

Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil. The delay is on the way back: structure collapses within the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year in the top 10 cm of soil with calcium carbonate, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on light soil, while soil without it is expected to recover more slowly (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–228, after the 1945 and 1953 floods in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay.
attributes.simplification: Folds Sodium on the clay, a stock between the two: the salt puts sodium on the clay, and the sodium breaks the clay's structure once the salt washes out. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes, and the stock's slowness is the link's delay. What one link distorts: the delay lies on the way back only, the structure collapsing within the first winter after the salt leaches out and recovering over years, while the link draws one delay for both ways.

attributes.description: Rain recharges the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, p. 233, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Within the year: the structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in. Whether what soaks in reaches the lens or leaves through the drains is set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674).

attributes.description: Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens, on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, and the Freshmaker and underground storage inject winter water through a deep drain or a well, all to pump in summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–22, 38, for the island). What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the permit (pp. 26, 45). Years to a decade, so a delay: on the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years and thickened the lens by up to 3.5 m (p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050); under a creek ridge on Walcheren, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, pp. 1424–1425, 1429, a model result, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R6: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so R6 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: With the same mortgage, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet, and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (van der Meulen et al., 2020). A high solvency makes new credit easier and cheaper to get; the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value.

Potatoes and onions are planted and sown in spring, and their soil work must not be done when the soil is too wet, which smears and compacts it and keeps an onion seedbed from forming; a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, from the Dutch cultivation guides). So the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring, which holding water back makes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Within the year.

Higher temperatures and drier weather raise evapotranspiration, the water crops use when they have enough, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56). Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.
attributes.simplification: Folds Crop water demand, a step between the two with no actor and no decision: hotter, drier summers raise what crops need, and what they need beyond the water they get is the shortfall. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: what crops need is no variable of its own, so a crop's own water need, new crops against the current ones, cannot enter; no source read shows whether the new crops need less.

So the more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall, within the season. On the island's farms a gift of 20 to 25 mm at germination makes the difference where none can be given now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 55).

attributes.description: Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the ditches are brackish to salt, and no water can be brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). They may pump only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, under the creek ridges and the dunes (p. 26): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not irrigate, while on a creek ridge a livestock farmer pumps from two deep drains for grassland through the summer, and an arable farmer irrigates about 20 mm at germination, the report not saying where that water comes from (pp. 27–28, 40, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. Within the year.

On the island it goes onto the field by reel sprinkler or by drip, and the method sets how much of it the crop gets: drip loses less water, so a cubic metre covers more land, while a reel usually gives several gifts per hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35, in its cost-benefit analysis for the island's farms). On a cluster of three farms on a creek ridge, a livestock farmer irrigates grassland in dry years, in midsummer too, from two deep drains under a permit of up to 16,000 m³ a year (pp. 40, 43). The salt a well may draw up with the water runs through Upconing of salt groundwater. Within the season: within the year, no delay.

attributes.description: A crop that uses less water than it needs yields less, in proportion: its relative yield falls by a crop's yield response factor times its relative shortfall in evapotranspiration, over the season 1.1 for potatoes and onions, 1.0 for sugar beet and 1.05 for winter wheat, the loss small in the vegetative and ripening periods and large in flowering and yield formation (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eq. 90 and Table 24, after FAO paper 33, general). On the island, farmers in the western low polders find the shortfall falls mostly at germination, and a crop that emerged well loses little to drought later in the summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27); a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his 2026 harvest, the potatoes smaller too, when growth stopped in the June heat and the rain came too late, his ditch water too saline to irrigate from (van Essen, 2026). Within the season.

The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the sooner the fields drain and dry after rain. By the water board's rules for its whole area, the drooglegging is set at an optimum for each use and soil, against both wet and drought damage (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); at half the design discharge it must keep a field's drains, laid at their optimal depth, all but above the ditch water (p. 8); and an area 10 cm or more short of its optimum counts as too wet (p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40), and the move from the winter to the summer level in spring follows the farmers' soil work (p. 66). Within the season, no delay.

Lower ditch levels lower the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater, so the seepage pressure rises; a higher level lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, the board's analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). The seepage is driven by the higher water pressure in the sand below the polders' clay (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year: the water pressures in the top layer change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: The water board names the gradually increasing salinisation a concern for the fresh water farming needs, the thin fresh groundwater lenses most threatened, and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses: by not lowering target levels much, since a lower level lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater and raises the seepage pressure, while a raise lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, a criterion of its analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17).

By the water board's rules, the views sent on a draft plan within six weeks are answered in the decision, anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it, and the board consults the region first so that as few conflicts as possible arise to slow or interrupt the procedure (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). So objections can delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels while it is pending; with none pending they change nothing, and they never lower a level. On the island the views on the two plans of 2021 changed neither: Duiveland's 25 views from six people (2021a, p. 53) and Schouwen's 11 from five, which added some studies (2021b, pp. 7–8). The only views against a raise, four on Duiveland's proposed study of one, gave as their reason the concern that flooding becomes likelier in extreme rain, not the land's value (2021a, p. 53); none of Schouwen's opposed the raises in its ten level areas (2021b, pp. 7–8, 53). The region's reactions before each draft were taken into the work on it (2021a, pp. 52–53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether anyone appealed either plan, no source read shows. Elsewhere in Zeeland a view did change the same board's plan: on the raise of a winter level in the Braakman, near Terneuzen, ZLTO objected for seven farmers that one party's gain should not harm another, and the plan of 2015 took a phased raise, its first step only once the field that suffers most has been acquired and its second within six years (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). Within the year, as the plan is decided.

Once a crop's root zone salinity, as the conductivity of the saturated soil extract (ECe), passes its threshold, its yield falls in proportion to the excess (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 89): onions lose 16% per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, rated sensitive and moderately sensitive, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Table 23), so on the island's rotations salt takes most from potatoes and onions. The harm is osmotic at once and comes from sodium or chloride building up in the leaves more slowly (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656). Table 23 is a guideline from experiments mostly under irrigation, tolerance varying with climate, soil and practice, and crops are often less tolerant as they germinate (Table 23, note 1): crop physiology that holds on the island's fields, its thresholds not measured there. Within the season.

Arable land needs lower ditch levels than grassland or nature. By the water board's rules for its whole area, a water level plan starts from an optimal level for each use and soil, the farmland's derived from the optimal drain depths for farming: for arable farming and horticulture 120 cm below the surface on salt-marsh clay (schorgronden) with no sand within 1.2 m, down to 60 on peat, for permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 7, 19), and for nature 0 cm as a general starting point, its levels set with the site managers, as Duiveland's analysis applied them to its land-use map of 2018 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29). So the more hectares farmed as arable land, the more land whose farmers need low levels, in spring as their soil work allows (2021a, p. 66); how strongly they ask for them, no source read shows (Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). Within the year: the need goes with the land's use each season, while the land leaves arable use only as it changes hands (Arable land in the polders).

Years, so a delay: the test runs as a plan is prepared, which the board does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: With more fresh water a farm keeps or takes on the crops that need it: on the island's low polders, with more fresh water available the farmer is open to more profitable crops and a more varied rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30). In Zeeland the area of sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 ha in 2024, the article naming the dry summers, the poor harvests and the lack of fresh water, four in five arable farmers having none, as farmers preferred less risky crops, while elsewhere the area grew (De Vriend, 2024, for Zeeland). Years, so a delay: farmers respond to the seasons they have had, and the fall ran over five years of dry summers.
attributes.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

attributes.description: The margin given up is net of what the new crop earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), so the better a new crop pays the less a farm gives up on each hectare it moves to it. Quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small (pp. 2–3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.
attributes.sources: Cloet, T., Van Meensel, J., De Boever, M., & Cnops, G. (2024). Rendabiliteit van de quinoateelt in Vlaanderen (Version September 2024). ILVO. https://ilvo.vlaanderen.be/uploads/documents/Projecten/Rendabiliteit-van-de-quinoateelt-in-Vlaanderen_sept2024.pdf

attributes.description: Banks look more and more at a farm's cash flow, whether its operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19): the bank judges whether the farmer can generate enough over the longer term for interest and repayment, the expected income being the limiting factor rather than the size of the farm (Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 3–4). Basel IV steers banks further toward profitability and liquidity rather than the value of collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). So the less a farm earns, the more risk its bank sees, for owner and tenant alike; for the Netherlands. Within the year.
attributes.sources:
van der Meulen, H., van der Meer, R., & van Asseldonk, M. (2020). Financiering transitie naar duurzame landbouw: Inzicht in het huidige financieringslandschap en ontwikkelingen (Rapport 2020-097). Wageningen Economic Research. https://edepot.wur.nl/532092
Farjon, H., Silvis, H., Vader, J., Voskuilen, M., & Agricola, H. (2013, December). Prijs hoger dan de waarde van landbouwgrond. Landwerk. PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency. https://www.pbl.nl/publicaties/prijs-hoger-dan-de-waarde-van-landbouwgrond

attributes.description: A public body can expropriate only for a use made possible in an adopted plan, a permit or a project decision (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.6), and only after a reasonable attempt to buy has failed (art. 11.7), so the more farmland planned for other uses, the more farmland within reach of an order. Years, so a delay: the attempt to buy and the order follow the adopted plan.
attributes.sources: Omgevingswet (version in force from 1 July 2026). https://wetten.overheid.nl/BWBR0037885/2026-07-01

attributes.label: R1 Salty soil takes in less rain
attributes.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium on the clay; once fresh water washes the salt out, the soil's structure collapses and recovers only over years. Less rain soaks in, less recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thins over years and saline groundwater comes closer to the roots: more salt. It runs in the low polders. The mechanism was measured after seawater floods; how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay, no source read shows. No practice is on it: the salt it adds drives tolerant crops and varieties (B13, B14).

attributes.label: R2 Growers and processors
attributes.description: More hectares under new salt-tolerant crops give more harvest within reach of a plant, which makes a local plant more worthwhile to buyers and processors. A plant nearby cuts transport, farmers keep more of the price, the crop is worth more and more farmers grow it. Run backwards, few hectares leave no reason for a plant and transport keeps the price low. It drives new crops once enough is grown and holds them back while too little is.

attributes.label: R3 Farm income and water storage
attributes.description: A farm with more left to invest can pay for more storage measures, so less winter rain drains away, more recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks, and yield, income and what the farm can invest rise. Run backwards, a farm with little left to invest cannot pay for storage, its water gets scarcer and its income falls further: the financial pressure R5 traces through what farms do, R3 traces through what they cannot do. It runs in the low polders. It drives storage on farms with the means and holds it back on farms without.

attributes.label: R4 Land value and bank credit
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, the same mortgage is more debt against the farm's assets, so banks see more risk and lend less. The farm has less to invest and moves fewer fields to new salt-tolerant crops, more of its conventional harvest stays exposed to salt, income falls and the land loses more value. It runs for farms that own their land. It shows an unintended consequence of the banks' response in B10: a bank limits its lending to protect itself, and farms that get less credit adapt less, which lowers the collateral further. It holds back new crops where land loses value and supports them where land keeps it.

attributes.label: R5 Leverage and deep drainage
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks charge a higher premium and its debt payments rise. To meet them it keeps its high-margin, salt-sensitive crops, whose spring soil work needs fields that dry early, so farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board, weighing that against raising them, plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, saline seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and leverage rises. It shows an unintended consequence of the deep drainage in B7: the gain comes within the season, the seepage and salt years later. It holds back new crops through the dependence it keeps up, while the salt it adds pushes towards them (B13, B14).

attributes.label: R6 Land value, objections and ditch levels
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, its owners may object harder to the next plan to raise ditch levels; whether they do is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the sign possibly opposite where compensation pays more than the land would fetch. Objections can hold today's level while a plan is pending, and never deepen it. Seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens stays thin, salt takes more of the harvest, income falls and the land loses more value. It shows an unintended consequence of the objections in B9: owners object to protect their land, and the levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower its value. It touches adoption through the salt it keeps up (B13, B14).

attributes.label: B2 Less arable land, less deep drainage
attributes.description: More salt in the root zone takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and where arable farming no longer pays for a buyer or successor the land goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land. With less arable land the water board, whose level follows the land's use, has more reason to raise the ditch levels, over years; seepage falls, the rainwater lens thickens and the salt falls back. It seeks the salt level at which arable farming stops paying for any successor or buyer, set by crop prices, margins and the land market. With B13 and B14 it is a way out of the same salt: those keep the land arable with another crop, this one is arable farming ending, where the current crops stop paying and adapting does not pay or is not chosen.

attributes.label: B3 Switching gives up margin
attributes.description: Moving a field to a new salt-tolerant crop gives up the current crop's margin, most on fresh land where the current crops still do well. Income and land value fall, leverage and the bank's risk rise, credit falls and the farm has less to invest, so fewer fields move. It seeks the share of new crops that a farm's income and credit can carry. It shares its chain with R4, where the switch saves harvest instead; a sign cannot say which pulls harder, so that is a question for the group. It holds back new crops.

attributes.label: B4 Storing water when harvests fall
attributes.description: As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile and those who can pay for it store more. Less winter rain drains away, the rainwater lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks and yields recover. It seeks the harvest at which storing stops being worth its cost, which each farmer sets against their other ways through a dry summer. It drives storage, slowly, the lens taking years to respond.

attributes.label: B5 Pumping relieves the shortfall
attributes.description: As the crop water shortfall grows, farmers pump more fresh groundwater, crops get more water and the shortfall shrinks, within the season. It seeks the water the crop needs, and runs only where a farm has fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick under it, on the creek ridges and dunes; the farmers talked to in the low polders do not irrigate. Where it eases the shortfall it eases the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B4), so it can hold storage back.

attributes.label: B7 Deep drainage keeps fields workable
attributes.description: Where fields stay too wet to work in spring, farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, the fields drain and dry sooner, and the wish for lower levels eases. It seeks fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring: what deep drainage gains a farm, R5 tracing what it costs. By keeping the current crops' spring work possible, it supports carrying on with them rather than adopting a practice.

attributes.label: B8 The water board raises levels against seepage
attributes.description: Lower ditch levels raise the saline seepage. The water board names the salinisation a concern and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses, so over years more seepage gives it more reason to plan raises; once carried out, the levels rise and the seepage falls. It seeks the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep; how far seepage weighs against drought in its plans, no source read shows. It touches adoption only through the salt it lowers (B13, B14).

attributes.label: B11 Pumping rules protect the lens
attributes.description: Under the creek ridges and dunes, the thicker the fresh groundwater, the more pumping the water board's rules allow. Farmers pump within that, and what they pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens. It seeks the balance between recharge and extraction on which the board set its limit. It shows an unintended consequence of the pumping in B5: a thinner lens, which reaches crops only through wells, so it comes back only through what the rules allow. For storage on the creek ridges, what infiltration adds to this lens is what wells can pump.

attributes.label: B12 The board tests the drainage depth
attributes.description: The water board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where little of the area is too wet a raise is considered, where much of it is the target level is lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved. Carried out over years, the depth moves back towards that optimum, which the board sets by its own rules. It touches adoption only through the seepage and salt the depth sets.

attributes.label: B9 Objections hold back plans
attributes.description: A plan to raise ditch levels brings objections, appeals and lobbying from landowning farmers who expect it to lower their land's value; whether that is their reason is a question for the group model building session. Objections can delay, change or stop the plan while it is pending, so fewer raises stay planned. It is the objectors' intended loop, protecting their land, and seeks a plan they can accept. It touches adoption only through the levels it holds, and through R6 and R9.

attributes.label: B10 Banks lend less as leverage rises
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks lend it less, less new debt is added and its leverage stops rising. It seeks the leverage a bank accepts, and is the banks' intended loop: they limit their exposure. By limiting credit it holds back what a farm can invest in new crops and storage; R4 shows what that can do in turn.

attributes.label: R9 Changed plans erode trust
attributes.description: Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans after public bodies have announced them. Plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one, their trust in government falls, and farmers who trust less object more. Both steps are hypotheses for the group model building session. It holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand, as trust falls.

attributes.label: R10 Capital ties farms to their crops
attributes.description: A farm tied to its current crops spends on keeping them as machines and stores fall due, over years. The more it owns for those crops, the more a switch to a new crop would write off, and what it would lose ties it further to them. It holds back new crops, and leaves tolerant varieties of the current crops nearly untouched.

attributes.label: R12 Storing teaches how storage works
attributes.description: The more measures are built and monitored on the island, the more its farmers, advisers and contractors know of how storage works there and what it costs, risks and yields, and the readier farmers are to invest. Run backwards, where farms do not invest nothing is learned and no knowledge base forms. It drives storage once measures are built and holds it back while few are. How long this takes, no source read shows.

attributes.label: B13 Salt losses move fields to new crops
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against the current crops, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A field moved no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take, so the harvest lost falls; the salt stays in the soil. It seeks the loss at which a farmer switches, which each farmer sets through their crops, margins, buyers and bank, a hypothesis for the group model building session. With B14 and B2 it is a way out of the same salt: switching keeps the land arable, B2 is arable farming ending. It drives new crops.

attributes.label: B14 Salt losses move fields to tolerant varieties
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the one grown now, so more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold. A tolerant variety loses less to salt, so the harvest lost falls. It seeks the loss at which a farmer changes variety, a hypothesis for the group model building session, as in B13. Tolerant varieties use the same machines, storage and know-how, so little capital is lost on them (R10). It drives tolerant varieties.

attributes.label: B15 Asking for a supply route
attributes.description: Farmers short of water, through their organisations, ask for a supply route, and the deciding body weighs it over the years a route takes to decide, pay for and build. A route would carry fresh water to the island, crops would have more to draw on and the shortfall would shrink. None exists, so the loop has not run yet; who decides and who pays is on the facts list under External freshwater supply. It seeks a shortfall the deciding body finds acceptable. Where it eased the shortfall it would ease the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B4).

attributes.label: B16 Expropriation, trust and the next plan
attributes.description: The more farmland the municipality plans for other uses, the more lies within reach of an expropriation order, after the attempt to buy has failed, over years. Expropriation lowers farmers' trust in government, farmers who trust less object more, and objections delay, change or stop the next plan, so less farmland is planned. It shows an unintended consequence of expropriating for a plan: the next plan becomes harder to adopt. It seeks the planned area the island's farmers will accept. The steps through trust are hypotheses for the group model building session. Through the trust it lowers it holds back storage.
